verses.text: One day Jonathan son of Saul said to the young man who carried his weapons, "Come, let us go over to the Philistine camp on the other side." But he did not tell his father.
Saul was staying on the edge of Gibeah under a pomegranate tree in Migron. About six hundred men were with him.
Among them was Ahijah, who was wearing an ephod. He was a son of Ichabod's brother Ahitub, son of Phinehas, son of Eli, the LORD's priest at Shiloh. No one knew that Jonathan had left.
On each side of the pass that Jonathan planned to cross to reach the Philistine camp there was a steep cliff. One was called Bozez and the other Seneh.
One cliff stood to the north toward Mikmash, the other to the south toward Geba.

Jonathan said to his young weapon carrier, "Come, let us go over to the camp of those uncircumcised men. Perhaps the LORD will act for us. Nothing can stop the LORD from saving, whether by many people or by few."
"Do all that you have in mind," his weapon carrier said. "Go ahead. I am with you heart and soul."
Jonathan said, "Come on, then. We will cross over toward the men and let them see us.
If they say to us, 'Wait there until we come to you,' we will stay where we are and not go up to them.
But if they say, 'Come up to us,' we will climb up, because that will be our sign that the LORD has given them into our hands."
So both of them showed themselves to the Philistine camp. "Look!" said the Philistines. "The Hebrews are crawling out of the holes they were hiding in."

The men of the camp shouted to Jonathan and his weapon carrier, "Come up to us and we will teach you a lesson." So Jonathan said to his weapon carrier, "Climb up after me. The LORD has given them into the hands of Israel."
Jonathan climbed up, using his hands and feet, with his weapon carrier right behind him. The Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his weapon carrier killed them behind him.
In that first attack Jonathan and his weapon carrier killed about twenty men in an area about half the size of a small field.
Then panic struck the whole Philistine army, in the camp and in the field. Even the soldiers in the camp and the raiding groups trembled. The ground shook. It was a panic sent by God.
Saul's lookouts at Gibeah in Benjamin saw the army running in every direction.
Then Saul said to the men with him, "Count the troops and see who has left us." When they counted, they found that Jonathan and his weapon carrier were missing.
Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the box of God here." At that time it was with the Israelites.
While Saul was talking to the priest, the noise in the Philistine camp grew louder and louder. So Saul said to the priest, "Stop what you are doing."
Then Saul and all his men gathered and went into battle. They found the Philistines in total confusion, striking each other with their swords.
Some Hebrews who had been with the Philistines before, and had gone up with them to their camp, now changed sides and joined the Israelites with Saul and Jonathan.
All the Israelites who had hidden in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were running away, and they joined the battle and chased after them.
So the LORD saved Israel that day, and the battle moved on past Beth Aven.

Now the Israelites were exhausted that day, because Saul had made the army take an oath, saying, "Cursed be anyone who eats food before evening comes, before I have taken revenge on my enemies!" So none of the troops tasted food.
The whole army entered the woods, and there was honey on the ground.
When they went into the woods, they saw the honey dripping, but no one dared to put any in their mouth, because they were afraid of the oath.

But Jonathan had not heard that his father had made the army take the oath. So he reached out the end of the stick in his hand and dipped it into the honeycomb. He raised his hand to his mouth, and his eyes brightened.
Then one of the soldiers told him, "Your father made the army take a strict oath, saying, 'Cursed be anyone who eats food today!' That is why the men are so weak."
Jonathan said, "My father has made trouble for the country. See how my eyes brightened when I tasted a little of this honey.
How much better it would have been if the men had eaten today some of the food they took from their enemies. Then we would have killed many more Philistines!"
That day, after the Israelites had struck down the Philistines from Mikmash to Aijalon, they were exhausted.
They rushed at the things they had taken and grabbed sheep, cattle and calves. They killed them on the ground and ate the meat with the blood still in it.
Then someone said to Saul, "Look, the men are sinning against the LORD by eating meat with blood still in it." "You have broken faith," Saul said. "Roll a large stone over here at once."

Then he said, "Go out among the men and tell them, 'Each of you bring me your cattle and sheep, and kill them here and eat them. Do not sin against the LORD by eating meat with blood still in it.'" So that night everyone brought his ox and killed it there.
Then Saul built an altar to the LORD. It was the first time he had built an altar to the LORD.

Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and rob them until dawn. Let us not leave one of them alive." "Do whatever seems best to you," they replied. But the priest said, "Let us ask God here first."
So Saul asked God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you give them into Israel's hands?" But God did not answer him that day.
Saul then said, "Come here, all you leaders of the army. Let us find out what sin has been done today.
As surely as the LORD who saves Israel lives, even if it was my son Jonathan, he must die." But not one of the men said a word.
Saul then said to all the Israelites, "You stand over there. I and my son Jonathan will stand over here." "Do what seems best to you," the men replied.
Then Saul prayed to the LORD, the God of Israel, "Show us the right answer." Jonathan and Saul were taken by the lot, and the men were cleared.
Saul said, "Cast the lot between me and Jonathan my son." And Jonathan was taken.
Then Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." So Jonathan told him, "I only tasted a little honey with the end of my stick. And now I must die!"
Saul said, "May God punish me severely if you do not die, Jonathan."

But the men said to Saul, "Should Jonathan die, the one who has won this great victory for Israel? Never! As surely as the LORD lives, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground, because he did this today with God's help." So the men rescued Jonathan, and he was not put to death.
Then Saul stopped chasing the Philistines, and they went back to their own land.
After Saul became king over Israel, he fought against his enemies on every side: Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he punished them.
He fought bravely and defeated the Amalekites, saving Israel from those who had robbed them.
Saul's sons were Jonathan, Ishvi and Malki-Shua. His older daughter was named Merab, and the younger one Michal.
His wife was Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. The commander of Saul's army was Abner son of Ner, who was Saul's uncle.
Saul's father Kish and Abner's father Ner were sons of Abiel.
All Saul's life there was bitter war with the Philistines. Whenever Saul saw a strong or brave man, he took him into his service.
